title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: neighbours, near and far
text:
This notebook builds the final submission from start to end. Every small area in the UK (LSOAs in England and Wales, Data Zones in Scotland, Super Data Zones in Northern Ireland) has an AlphaEarth embedding for 2024: 64 numbers summarising a year of satellite observations. We compare every pair of neighbouring areas and turn three of them into Polaroid cards:
The exploration behind these choices lives in gdsl30dmc.ipynb and gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb; this notebook depends only on the shared module gdsl30dmc_tools.py (data loading, contiguity and the Polaroid card template).

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: neighbours, near and far
text:
Setup
Libraries for the whole pipeline. The shared module also registers the card fonts: Figtree for the caption and Special Elite, a typewriter face, for the haiku.


code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

import gdsl30dmc_tools as tools

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: neighbours, near and far
text:
Areas and their neighbours
We read the 2024 areas with their mean embeddings and connect every pair of areas whose polygons touch or overlap (fuzzy contiguity: queen contiguity plus the England–Scotland border, where the two nations’ polygons overlap). Twelve island areas have no neighbours, so we drop them.


code
%%time
YEAR = 2024
areas = tools.load_areas(YEAR)
g = tools.contiguity(areas)
areas, g = tools.drop_isolates(areas, g)
print(f"{len(areas):,} areas | {g.n_edges // 2:,} neighbouring pairs")

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: neighbours, near and far
section: How different is each pair of neighbours?
text:
How different is each pair of neighbours?
For every neighbouring pair we compute the cosine distance between their embeddings: 0 means the two areas look the same to the model, and larger values mean more different. We compute it from scratch here (cache=None) rather than reading the copy cached by the exploration notebooks. Each pair appears once, with its two codes in alphabetical order.


code
dist = tools.pair_distances(areas, g, cache=None)
km2 = areas.area / 1e6
pairs = dist.reset_index().assign(km2_a=lambda d: km2[d.a].to_numpy(), km2_b=lambda d: km2[d.b].to_numpy())
pairs.dist.describe().round(4)

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: neighbours, near and far
text:
Picking the three pairs

Most different: the pair with the largest distance.
Most similar: the pair with the smallest distance.
Most similar urban: the smallest distance among pairs where both areas cover between 0.05 and 1 km². Areas are drawn to hold similar numbers of people, so small areas are urban. The lower bound leaves out tiny areas, whose average embedding rests on only a few hundred 10 m pixels and is less reliable.

On each card, the larger of the two areas is outlined in orange and the other in green.


code
URBAN_KM2 = (0.05, 1.0)
urban = pairs.km2_a.between(*URBAN_KM2) & pairs.km2_b.between(*URBAN_KM2)

picks = pd.DataFrame({
    "most_different": pairs.loc[pairs.dist.idxmax()],
    "most_similar": pairs.loc[pairs.dist.idxmin()],
    "most_similar_urban": pairs[urban].loc[pairs[urban].dist.idxmin()],
}).T
swap = picks.km2_b > picks.km2_a  # larger area first, so it is drawn in orange
picks.loc[swap, ["a", "b", "km2_a", "km2_b"]] = picks.loc[swap, ["b", "a", "km2_b", "km2_a"]].to_numpy()
picks["rank_different"] = [int((dist > d).sum()) + 1 for d in picks.dist]
picks["rank_similar"] = [int((dist < d).sum()) + 1 for d in picks.dist]

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: neighbours, near and far
text:
Captions
Each card carries a place name and a haiku in place of statistics. Place names were checked by reverse-geocoding each area’s centre with OpenStreetMap (Nominatim):

E01030745 contains Staines Reservoirs, and E01030710 is the housing of neighbouring Stanwell (Spelthorne, Surrey).
The Armagh pair lies between Richhill and Hamiltonsbawn.
The Ilford pair lies in Loxford and Seven Kings, London Borough of Redbridge (IG1).

The expect codes guard the captions: if the data or the rules ever change and a different pair is picked, the notebook stops instead of printing the wrong poem on a new picture.


code
N = len(dist)
CAPTIONS = {
    "most_different": dict(
        expect={"E01030745", "E01030710"}, place="Staines Reservoirs, Surrey",
        rank=lambda r: f"#1 most different of {N:,}",
        haiku="Still black reservoir —\nthe next street hangs out washing.\nNothing more apart."),
    "most_similar": dict(
        expect={"N20000681", "N20000689"}, place="Farmland, County Armagh",
        rank=lambda r: f"#1 most similar of {N:,}",
        haiku="Green field, hedge, green field.\nA map line says they are two;\nthe land knows just one."),
    "most_similar_urban": dict(
        expect={"E01003685", "E01003730"}, place="Ilford, east London",
        rank=lambda r: f"most similar urban pair (#{r.rank_similar} of {N:,})",
        haiku="Same bay window, same\nchimney pots, same Tuesday bins.\nTwo codes, one long street."),
}
for kind, r in picks.iterrows():
    assert {r.a, r.b} == CAPTIONS[kind]["expect"], f"{kind}: picked {r.a}–{r.b}, captions were written for another pair"

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: neighbours, near and far
text:
The cards
Each card is a Polaroid: Esri satellite imagery washed out except over the two areas, the pair’s codes as the title, the place, distance and rank underneath, the haiku in a typewriter face, and a UK locator. Cards are saved at 200 dpi to figures/submission/.


code
%%time
uk_outline = tools.uk_outline(areas)
out_dir = tools.FIG_DIR / "submission"
for i, (kind, r) in enumerate(picks.iterrows(), 1):
    cap = CAPTIONS[kind]
    d = f"{r.dist:.3f}" if r.dist >= 0.01 else f"{r.dist:.4f}"
    subtitle = f"{cap['place']}  ·  distance {d}  ·  {cap['rank'](r)}"
    fig = tools.pair_card(areas, r.a, r.b, subtitle, uk_outline, haiku=cap["haiku"])
    print(tools.export_card(fig, f"{i}_{kind}", fig_dir=out_dir).relative_to(tools.ROOT))
    plt.show()

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: neighbours, near and far
text:
Post text
The text for the LinkedIn post that goes with the three cards. It’s kept in a plain-text block so the hashtags don’t render as headings and it can be copied as is.
#30DayMapChallenge, day 10: prompting only.

Every small area in the UK (46,832 of them) has a 2024 AlphaEarth embedding, made available through Imago: 64 numbers that sum up a year of satellite observations. Compare each area with the ones it touches and you get 136,233 pairs of neighbours, ranked from most different to most alike.

Three of them:

1. The most different: Staines Reservoirs and the streets of Stanwell next door.
2. The most alike: two stretches of farmland in County Armagh.
3. The most alike in a city: two halves of the same terraced streets in Ilford.

The first is the one you'd guess. The other two are more interesting: the boundaries we use to count people often split places that, as far as the satellites can tell, are the same place.

Everything here (the data processing, the maps, even the haiku) came from prompting Claude Code. No code written by hand.

#30DayMapChallenge #GeographicDataScience

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: “Prompting only”
text: Where in the UK do neighbouring small areas look most unlike each other from space? This notebook measures dissimilarity between contiguous LSOAs (and their Scottish/NI equivalents) using the distance between their 2024 AlphaEarth satellite-embedding vectors, aggregated by Imago.

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: “Prompting only”
text:
Setup
The libraries used throughout: geopandas for the polygons and embeddings, libpysal’s new Graph for contiguity, scikit-learn for cosine distances, and joblib to compute them in parallel. autoreload picks up edits to the shared gdsl30dmc_tools.py module without restarting the kernel.


code

%autoreload 2

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from joblib import Parallel, delayed
from libpysal import graph
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import paired_cosine_distances

print(gpd.__version__)

nation = pd.Series(lsoas.index.str[0], index=lsoas.index)

def link_types(g):
    """Count directed links by nation pair, ignoring isolates' zero-weight self-loops."""
    adj = g.adjacency.reset_index()
    adj = adj[adj.focal != adj.neighbor]
    return pd.Series(nation.loc[adj.focal].values + "-" + nation.loc[adj.neighbor].values).value_counts()

Fixing the England–Scotland border
Only one England–Scotland pair is linked, even though about two dozen pairs of areas meet along that border. The two nations’ polygons slightly overlap there (by up to ~70,000 m²), and contiguity only counts polygons that touch without overlapping. Fuzzy contiguity links any pair of geometries that intersect, which covers touching (queen) and overlapping polygons alike, so it fixes the border without adding spurious links elsewhere.


code
%%time
g = graph.Graph.build_fuzzy_contiguity(lsoas)

edges = lambda g: set(g.adjacency[g.adjacency > 0].index)
print("Links only in queen:", len(edges(g_queen) - edges(g)), "| only in fuzzy:", len(edges(g) - edges(g_queen)))
link_types(g)

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: “Prompting only”
text:
Neighbour dissimilarity
We measure how different each area is from each of its neighbours using cosine distance between their 2024 embedding vectors (1 − cosine similarity, from 0 for identical directions to 2 for opposite). Cosine ignores vector length, which in these area averages partly reflects how mixed the land cover is, and is the comparison AlphaEarth embeddings are designed for. Neighbours come from the fuzzy-contiguity graph g, i.e. queen contiguity plus the overlapping England–Scotland border pairs.
The 46,832 areas are split into 16 groups (one per core), and each group’s distances to all its neighbours are computed on a separate thread. NumPy releases Python’s global interpreter lock while it computes, so threads share the arrays without copying them. The results are reassembled into the order of g.adjacency and stored as the weights of a new graph, g_dist.


code
%%time
N_CHUNKS = 16
emb = np.ascontiguousarray(emb)  # row-major, so gathering whole rows is fast (~4x here)

adj = g.adjacency
i = lsoas.index.get_indexer(adj.index.get_level_values("focal"))  # row of each focal area in emb
j = lsoas.index.get_indexer(adj.index.get_level_values("neighbor"))

# Assign each area to one of N_CHUNKS groups, then find the links whose focal area is in each group
area_chunk = np.repeat(np.arange(N_CHUNKS), [len(c) for c in np.array_split(np.arange(len(lsoas)), N_CHUNKS)])
link_chunk = area_chunk[i]
rows = [np.flatnonzero(link_chunk == k) for k in range(N_CHUNKS)]

parts = Parallel(n_jobs=N_CHUNKS, backend="threading")(
    delayed(paired_cosine_distances)(emb[i[r]], emb[j[r]]) for r in rows
)
dist = np.empty(len(adj))
for r, d in zip(rows, parts):
    dist[r] = d

g_dist = graph.Graph(pd.Series(dist, index=adj.index, name="weight"))

Wall time: 865 ms

assert np.allclose(dist, paired_cosine_distances(emb[i], emb[j]))
assert g_dist.n_edges == g.n_edges and (g_dist.unique_ids == g.unique_ids).all()

Dissimilarity from the whole neighbourhood
Two ways to score how different an area is from its neighbourhood as a whole, using equal weights for every neighbour:

mean_dist: the average of the cosine distances to each neighbour, i.e. how different the area is from its neighbours one by one. Taken from the weights of g_dist.
lag_dist: the cosine distance to the average neighbour, i.e. how different the area is from its surroundings taken together. The average neighbour is the spatial lag of the embeddings on the row-standardised graph.

Since averaging neighbours tends to cancel out their differences, lag_dist should be at most mean_dist for nearly every area. The gap between the two is roughly how much the neighbours differ among themselves.


code
emb_lag = g.transform("r").lag(emb)  # row i = mean embedding of area i's neighbours

neighbourhood = pd.DataFrame({
    "mean_dist": g_dist.aggregate("mean").reindex(lsoas.index),
    "lag_dist": paired_cosine_distances(emb, emb_lag),
}, index=lsoas.index)

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: “Prompting only”
text:
Mapping the most dissimilar areas
Each area becomes a Polaroid-style card. A square satellite photo (Esri imagery, no API key needed) shows the focal area outlined in orange and its neighbours in green, with everything outside them washed out towards white. Below it, a caption strip carries the area code and its scores in bold Figtree, Imago’s brand font, plus a UK silhouette locating the area. Colours follow Imago’s brand palette: Orange #FF8F42, Green #03CEA3, and Imago Grey #4A4A49 for the text and the UK silhouette.
The card template, the UK silhouette and the export helper live in gdsl30dmc_tools.py, shared with the other notebooks. The silhouette is built by merging each nation’s areas, using GEOS’s fast coverage_union where the polygons tile cleanly, then simplifying. It takes about 25 s and is cached to data/uk_outline.parquet, so it’s only built once.


code
%%time
import gdsl30dmc_tools as tools

uk_outline = tools.uk_outline(lsoas)


CPU times: user 25.7 s, sys: 510 ms, total: 26.2 s
Wall time: 26.2 s




code
def plot_focal(code):
    """Card for area `code` (orange) and its neighbours (green), captioned with its neighbourhood scores."""
    s = neighbourhood.loc[code]
    subtitle = f"mean_dist {s.mean_dist:.3f}  ·  lag_dist {s.lag_dist:.3f}  ·  {g.cardinalities[code]} neighbours"
    return tools.area_card(lsoas, code, g.neighbors[code], subtitle, uk_outline)


def plot_pair(a, b):
    """Card for neighbouring areas `a` (orange) and `b` (green), captioned with their cosine distance."""

title: Neighbours, near and far
text:
Every small area in the UK, all 46,832 of them, has a 2024 AlphaEarth embedding, made available by Imago: 64 numbers that sum up a year of satellite observations of the place. Compare each area with the ones it touches and you get 136,233 pairs of neighbours, which we can rank from most different to most alike.
These are three of them.
The most different: Staines Reservoirs and the streets of Stanwell next door, #1 of 136,233 pairs. The most alike: two stretches of farmland in County Armagh. The most alike in a city: two halves of the same terraced streets in Ilford.
The first is the one you’d guess. The other two are more interesting: the boundaries we use to count people often split places that, as far as the satellites can tell, are the same place.

title: Neighbours, near and far
text:
Reading a card
Each card is a Polaroid of one pair of neighbouring areas. The two areas are outlined in orange and green over Esri satellite imagery, and everything else is washed out. Underneath are the areas’ official codes, the place, the cosine distance between their embeddings (0 means identical; the largest in the UK is 0.538) and its rank among all pairs. The UK locator shows where the pair is. The haiku says what the numbers can’t.

1 · The brief
The project started from a short brief, SPEC.md: map the UK’s most dissimilar neighbouring small areas, measuring similarity with AlphaEarth embeddings from Imago, using geopandas and PySAL’s new Graph, and keeping a log of explorations.

title: Backstory
text:
2 · Who touches whom
Before comparing neighbours, we need to know who the neighbours are. Queen contiguity (areas sharing at least a corner) across all four nations gave a graph with one surprise: no links at all across the England–Scotland border, because the two nations’ polygons overlap rather than touch. Fuzzy contiguity, which also counts overlaps, fixed that with 21 extra links. Twelve island areas had no neighbours at all and were dropped.

# #30DayMapChallenge, Submission Day 10

> "Prompting only" - For this map, make AI work for its money and produce something
from start to finish in a chat window or on the command line.

We are going to be working towards building a submission for this day. The
idea is to create a map of the areas in the UK with the most dissimilar
neighboring LSOAs. We will measure similarity with AlphaEarth embeddings, and
areas with official LSOA polygons. 

## Data

We are going to be working with Imago's embeddings product:

> https://data.imago.ac.uk/datasets/google-satellite-embedding-v1-small-areas-2017-2024

We will start playing with 2024, but we might explore looking at change later
on.

## Similarity

In this context, we will describe similarity of two LSOAs as the distance 
between their two embedding vectors.

We might also explore a variation where we compute similarity between a given
LSOA and _all_ of its surrounding neighbors.

## Tools

We will, at least, rely on geopandas for working with the data, and PySAL for
working with topology/contiguity. Please examine the documentation for the
migration to the new `Graph` structure for spatial weights:

> https://pysal.org/libpysal/stable/user-guide/graph/w_g_migration.html

I’ve read the spec, created gdsl30dmc.ipynb with a Setup section and a Reading data section, and run it. Everything executes without errors.
What’s in the 2024 data:

46,844 small areas covering the whole UK: 33,755 in England, 7,392 in Scotland, 3,780 in Northern Ireland and 1,917 in Wales. Scotland’s areas are Data Zones and Northern Ireland’s are Super Data Zones, not LSOAs, so “LSOA” here really means the small-area unit used in each nation.
Columns: the data_zone_code ID, 64 columns band1_mean…band64_mean, and the polygons, already in British National Grid. No values are missing.
The vectors aren’t unit length: their lengths range from 0.75 to 0.99. AlphaEarth gives every pixel a unit-length vector, so averaging them over an area shrinks the result, and it shrinks more the more mixed the area’s land cover is. That bears on how we measure distance, below.
Harmless warning: the read cell prints a PROJ “Open of …/share/proj failed” error. The CRS still resolves correctly (EPSG:27700), so you can ignore it.

Decisions before the contiguity and similarity section:

Coverage: keep all four nations, or only Great Britain? Northern Ireland doesn’t touch the rest, so it would be its own block of neighbours either way.
Contiguity: I’d use queen, where areas sharing a corner count as neighbours, via graph.Graph.build_contiguity(lsoas, rook=False). Islands with no neighbours, such as Scilly and parts of the Hebrides, would be flagged and dropped.
Distance: I’d use Euclidean distance, as SPEC.md says. Cosine distance is the alternative: it compares only the direction of the vectors, so it ignores the shrinkage from mixed land cover. I’d add it as a quick comparison.
How to map it: the first map could colour each area by the mean distance to its neighbours, which is the “all surrounding neighbours” idea in SPEC.md. The alternative is to draw the shared boundaries themselves, coloured by how different the two areas on each side are. The boundary version is more literal and probably makes the more striking map.

    Generate Graph from fuzzy contiguity

    Fuzzy contiguity relaxes the notion of contiguity neighbors

**Final graph `g`:** 272,466 links, median 6 neighbours per area (max 53), **12 areas with no neighbours**,

#10 · Wed 4 Nov, 12:20cosine perhaps?

Yes, I’d use cosine distance (1 − cosine similarity) as the main measure.
Why cosine fits these vectors:

It’s how AlphaEarth embeddings are meant to be compared. Each pixel’s vector has length 1, and Google’s guidance is to compare them with the dot product, which for unit-length vectors is the same as cosine similarity.
Averaging muddles the vector lengths. Our area vectors are averages of pixel vectors, so their lengths (0.75–0.99) partly reflect how mixed an area’s land cover is. Cosine ignores length and compares only direction, which here means the overall land-cover mix. Euclidean distance would also count a difference in mixedness: a uniform field next to a patchwork of fields with the same overall mix would look different.
It’s easy to read. Values run from 0 (same direction) to 2 (opposite).

How much it matters: probably not much. If you rescale each vector to length 1 first, squared Euclidean distance becomes exactly 2 × cosine distance, so the two give the same ranking. On the raw averages they can only differ through vector length, and those lengths vary little (standard deviation 0.034).
What I’d suggest:

Compute cosine distance for every pair of neighbouring areas, stored on the graph so we can map shared borders later.
As a quick check, also compute raw Euclidean distance and report how closely the two rankings agree (Spearman correlation). If they agree, we keep cosine and note that the choice didn’t matter much. If they don’t, the areas where they differ are worth mapping.
Hold off on combining the pairs into a single score per area (mean or max over its neighbours) until you’ve seen the pair-level distribution.

The calculation:

Take the neighbour pairs from g.adjacency, which is indexed by focal and neighbor: 272,466 rows, with each pair of neighbours appearing once in each direction.
Look up both areas’ 64-band vectors and compute cosine distance for every pair in one go with sklearn.metrics.pairwise.paired_cosine_distances(emb[i], emb[j]). That’s about 17 million multiplications, which takes milliseconds. Doing it by hand (normalise each row to length 1, then 1 minus the row-wise dot product) gives the same result.
Keep the results on the graph: a new graph g_dist, built with the same links as g but with the cosine distance as each link’s weight. That lets us use the Graph machinery later, for example to average over each area’s neighbours, and it gives us the pairs needed to map shared borders.

Why not parallelise:

The work is one vectorised operation over a 272k × 64 array. Starting worker processes and copying data to them would take longer than the calculation itself.
NumPy already uses compiled code for this kind of array maths.
The slow parts of this workflow are building the graph (about 3 s) and plotting, not the distances.

## Neighbour dissimilarity

We measure how different each area is from each of its neighbours using **cosine distance** between their 2024 embedding vectors (1 − cosine similarity, from 0 for identical directions to 2 for opposite). Cosine ignores vector length, which in these area averages partly reflects how mixed the land cover is, and is the comparison AlphaEarth embeddings are designed for. Neighbours come from the fuzzy-contiguity graph `g`, i.e. queen contiguity plus the overlapping England–Scotland border pairs.

The 46,832 areas are split into 16 groups (one per core), and each group's distances to all its neighbours are computed on a separate thread. NumPy releases Python's global interpreter lock while it computes, so threads share the arrays without copying them. The results are reassembled into the order of `g.adjacency` and stored as the weights of a new graph, `g_dist`.
@@code
%%time
from joblib import Parallel, delayed
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import paired_cosine_distances

N_CHUNKS = 16

adj = g.adjacency
focal = adj.index.get_level_values("focal")
i = lsoas.index.get_indexer(focal)  # row of each focal area in emb
j = lsoas.index.get_indexer(adj.index.get_level_values("neighbor"))

# Rows of adj belonging to each group of focal areas
rows = [np.flatnonzero(focal.isin(codes)) for codes in np.array_split(lsoas.index, N_CHUNKS)]

parts = Parallel(n_jobs=N_CHUNKS, backend="threading")(
    delayed(paired_cosine_distances)(emb[i[r]], emb[j[r]]) for r in rows
)
dist = np.empty(len(adj))
for r, d in zip(rows, parts):
    dist[r] = d

g_dist = graph.Graph(pd.Series(dist, index=adj.index, name="weight"))

#18 · Wed 4 Nov, 13:23ok now let's think about how a distance between the focal area and its neighbors would work. Two thoughts: 1) we get the distances between i and every j in the neighborhood, and then average it; 2) we average the embedding of the neighbors and then the distance. Thoughts?

Both are reasonable, but they measure different things. I’d compute both, since each takes a line or two and they’re more useful side by side.
1. Average of the distances, mean(d(i, j)): “how different is this area from each of its neighbours, on average?”

It counts an area as dissimilar when it differs from its neighbours one by one. That includes areas that sit between neighbours that differ from each other.
Example: a farmland area with town on one side and moorland on the other scores high, even if farmland is a fair halfway point between the two.
It uses g_dist directly: the mean of each area’s distances to its neighbours.

2. Distance to the averaged neighbour, d(i, mean(j)): “how different is this area from its surroundings taken as a whole?”

This is the embedding version of a spatial lag: the row-standardised graph’s lag applied to emb gives one averaged vector per area, which is then compared with the area’s own vector.
Differences among the neighbours tend to cancel out in the average, so the farmland example above scores lower. What scores high is a genuine outlier: an area unlike anything around it, like E01030745 from the last table.
One subtlety: averaging very different neighbours gives a blurred, mixed vector. A mixed area of its own can then look close to its surroundings even though it matches none of them individually.

How they relate: with these embeddings, option 2 should come out at or below option 1 for nearly every area. The gap between them roughly measures how much the neighbours differ from each other. That gives three useful cases:
Option 1 | Option 2 | Reading |
|—|—|—|
high | high | outlier, unlike all of its surroundings |
high | low | sits between neighbours that differ from each other (an edge or transition) |
low | low | uniform neighbourhood |
Weighting: both options give every neighbour equal weight. One alternative is weighting by the length of shared boundary, using build_contiguity(..., by_perimeter=True) on our graph. Another, for option 2 only, is weighting by neighbour area, so that the averaged neighbour reflects the actual land around the area. I’d start unweighted and revisit if small slivers of neighbouring areas turn out to distort results.
Recommendation: if we need one number for “most dissimilar area” maps, I’d use option 2, since it matches “unlike its surroundings” and is less sensitive to one odd neighbour. I’d also compute option 1, compare the two in a scatter plot, and look at the cases where they disagree.

Option 1: average of the pairwise distances
The distances are already stored as the weights of g_dist, so this is just a mean per area:

Option 2: distance to the averaged neighbour

emb_lag = g_r.lag(emb)    # (46,832 × 64): average embedding of each area's neighbours
lag_dist = paired_cosine_distances(emb, emb_lag)

lag(emb) returns a 46,832 × 64 array whose row i is the mean of the vectors of i’s neighbours. Underneath, this is one sparse matrix product, g_r.sparse @ emb.
Row i of emb_lag lines up with row i of emb, because we checked earlier that g.unique_ids matches lsoas.index.
We use g, not g_dist, since the averaging needs equal weights, not distances.

Two per-area scores, with equal weights for every neighbour: `mean_dist` = mean of the cosine distances to each neighbour
(`g_dist.aggregate("mean")`); `lag_dist` = cosine distance to the average neighbour embedding

0.438. In the scatter plot, areas near the diagonal are outliers (unlike all their surroundings); areas well below it are
transitions (their neighbours differ from each other). Also built `most_dissimilar`: each area's single most dissimilar
neighbour and the distance to it.

CARD_W, BORDER, STRIP = 8, 0.45, 1.6
CARD_H = CARD_W + STRIP


def plot_focal(code):
    """Polaroid-style satellite card of area `code` and its neighbours, surroundings washed out, with a UK locator."""
    focal = lsoas.loc[[code], ["geometry"]]

    h, w = rgb.shape[:2]
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(ext[0], ext[1], w), np.linspace(ext[3], ext[2], h))
    inside = shapely.contains_xy(pd.concat([focal, nbrs]).union_all(), xx, yy)[..., None]
    rgb = np.where(inside, rgb, rgb * (1 - WASH) + WASH)

Both ideas are worth trying, and they combine well: the clusters give us a vocabulary of land types, and the city filter narrows where we look. I’d start with idea 2, because it needs no extra data and directly tackles the “built-up versus open land every time” problem.
Idea 1: restrict to cities

Pros: cheap once we have boundaries, and it should surface urban contrasts: a park against dense terraces, docks against housing, a rail yard against a housing estate.
Needs city boundaries, which we don’t have. Options:

Recommended: the ONS lookup from areas to local authorities, which lets us filter on, say, the 33 London boroughs or Liverpool. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own equivalent lookups.
More precise: ONS built-up area polygons, which match where a city physically ends rather than its administrative edge.
Quickest: a radius around each city centre. No download, but crude.

Caveat: cities contain parks, reservoirs and rivers, so built-up-versus-open contrasts won’t disappear. They’ll just be urban ones. The reservoir isn’t technically in London: it’s in Spelthorne, just outside it.

Idea 2: cluster, then search at the cluster level

a. Clustering: k-means with k=100 on the 64-band embeddings takes seconds at this size. I’d first scale each vector to length 1. That makes k-means effectively cluster by cosine similarity, matching the distance we’ve used so far.
b. Interpreting clusters: there’s no land-cover label to check against, so interpretation has to be visual. For each cluster, I’d make a contact sheet of satellite thumbnails of its 9 most typical areas, which suits the Polaroid theme.

Labelling 100 by eye is a lot of work. I’d also merge the 100 clusters into about 10–15 families, using Ward clustering on their centres, so we can label families first and drill in where it matters.
My labels would be guesses read from the imagery, so you’d want to sanity-check them.

c. Searching by cluster: this is where it gets interesting. Two ways:

One example per contrast type: label every neighbouring pair by its two clusters, then keep only the most extreme pair for each cluster combination. The final ranking then spans different kinds of contrast instead of 20 variations on housing next to water. “The industrial estate next to the most different landscape” is a filter on this: pairs where one side is an industrial-looking cluster, ranked by distance.
Surprising neighbours: count how often each pair of clusters actually sits side by side, compared with chance. Clusters that are adjacent less often than expected, or never, point to unusual juxtapositions, which is a different notion of “interesting” from raw distance.

Caveat: two-thirds of the areas are English LSOAs, mostly urban, so many of the 100 clusters will be shades of residential. That’s fine, as it’s exactly what we need to tell urban types apart.

What this says:

No natural number of clusters: silhouette falls steadily as k grows, with no peak and no elbow. The embeddings form continuous gradients (rural → suburban → dense urban), so any k is a way of slicing a continuum. Statistics won’t settle it; interpretability should.
Rare land types appear somewhere between k=40 and k=50: the smallest cluster drops from 315 areas to 89. A tiny cluster at higher k is likely a rare type such as water, airports, quarries or large industrial sites. Those rare types are exactly what makes a contrast interesting, so we shouldn’t lose them entirely.

Labelling is feasible: 20 clusters can be checked by eye in an afternoon. At 100 we’d be guessing.
The contrast types stay manageable: 20 clusters give 190 possible pairs of cluster types, few enough to browse. 100 give 4,950.
Every cluster is substantial, with at least 835 areas, so each label describes something common.

@@markdown
## Choosing the number of clusters

Before fixing k, we fit k-means for a range of values and record two things: the silhouette score (how well separated the clusters are, from −1 to 1, computed with cosine distance on a 10,000-area sample) and the size of the smallest cluster. There's no single right k here: the aim is a number of groups we can label by eye that still keeps rare land types visible.
@@code
%%time
KS = [5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 75, 100]
sample = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(emb_unit), 10_000, replace=False)

rows = []
for k in KS:
    labels = KMeans(k, n_init=3, random_state=0).fit_predict(emb_unit)
    sizes = np.bincount(labels)
    rows.append({"k": k, "silhouette": silhouette_score(emb_unit[sample], labels[sample], metric="cosine"),
                 "smallest": sizes.min(), "largest": sizes.max()})
k_scan = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("k")
k_scan.round(3)
@@code

k_scan["smallest"].plot(ax=ax2, marker="o", color=tools.IMAGO["orange"], logy=True)
ax2.set_ylabel("Smallest cluster (areas, log scale)")
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.axvline(20, color=tools.IMAGO["dark_grey"], ls="--", lw=0.8)

@@markdown
## Clustering the embeddings

We fit k-means at two levels: **k=20** for the main land types we'll label by eye, and **k=100** for a finer split that should separate rarer types. We use 10 random starts per fit for stability, and number the clusters in each level by size (0 = largest), so the numbering stays meaningful. The labels are saved to `data/clusters_2024.parquet` for reuse.
@@code
%%time
def fit_kmeans(k, seed=0):
    km = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=seed).fit(emb_unit)
    order = np.argsort(-np.bincount(km.labels_))  # old label of the largest cluster first
    relabel = np.empty(k, int)
    relabel[order] = np.arange(k)
    return relabel[km.labels_], km.cluster_centers_[order]

c20, centres20 = fit_kmeans(20)
c100, centres100 = fit_kmeans(100)
clusters = pd.DataFrame({"c20": c20, "c100": c100}, index=lsoas.index)
clusters.to_parquet(tools.DATA_DIR / f"clusters_{YEAR}.parquet")

print("k=20 sizes:", np.bincount(c20).tolist())
print("k=100 sizes: min", np.bincount(c100).min(), "| median", int(np.median(np.bincount(c100))), "| max", np.bincount(c100).max())
@@markdown
### How the two levels nest

k-means fits the two levels independently, so a fine cluster need not sit inside a single coarse one. For each k=100 cluster, we record which k=20 cluster most of its areas belong to and how large that share is. High shares mean the fine level mostly subdivides the coarse one, which makes the two levels easier to read together.
@@code
nest = pd.crosstab(clusters.c100, clusters.c20)
fine = pd.DataFrame({
    "size": nest.sum(axis=1),
    "main_c20": nest.idxmax(axis=1),
    "share": (nest.max(axis=1) / nest.sum(axis=1)).round(2),
})
print("Share of each k=100 cluster inside its main k=20 cluster:")
print(fine["share"].describe().round(2).to_string())
print("\nk=100 clusters per k=20 cluster:")
print(fine.groupby("main_c20").size().to_string())

@@markdown
## What the clusters look like

To interpret each k=20 cluster, we look at its six most typical areas: those whose embedding is closest (highest cosine similarity) to the cluster centre. Each is shown as a satellite thumbnail with the area outlined and its surroundings washed out. The sheets are saved to `figures/clusters/` so we can review them side by side and agree labels.
@@code
def typical(level_labels, centres, cluster, n=6):
    """Codes of the n areas in `cluster` closest to its centre (cosine similarity)."""
    members = np.flatnonzero(level_labels == cluster)
    centre = centres[cluster] / np.linalg.norm(centres[cluster])
    best = members[np.argsort(-(emb_unit[members] @ centre))[:n]]
    return lsoas.index[best].tolist()

typical20 = {c: typical(c20, centres20, c) for c in range(20)}

This is the contact sheet for k=20 cluster 18, the one I drafted as “city centres”. It has 1,180 areas, and the sheet shows the 6 closest to the cluster centre. The file is figures/clusters/c20_18.png.
On closer inspection, “city centres” is a bit too strong a label:

What they share: small areas (0.08–0.40 km²) that are almost fully built up, with large flat-roofed blocks, flats, offices and institutional buildings. There are hardly any gardens and little of the regular terraced pattern you see in clusters 15 and 16.
Not all are central business districts:

The top-left area sits beside what looks like a football stadium.
Top-right and bottom-middle are on a waterfront or docks.
Several look like dense inner-city mixed use: council blocks, campuses and offices.

def pair_distances(areas=None, g=None, cache=DATA_DIR / "pair_distances_2024.parquet"):
    """Cosine distance for every neighbouring pair (each pair once, a < b), cached to disk.

    Without `areas` and `g`, loads the cache (or builds it from the 2024 data, dropping isolates).
    """
    if cache is not None and Path(cache).exists():
        return pd.read_parquet(cache)["dist"]
    if areas is None or g is None:
        areas = load_areas()
        areas, g = drop_isolates(areas, contiguity(areas))
    adj = g.adjacency.reset_index()
    adj = adj[adj["focal"] < adj["neighbor"]]
    emb = areas[band_columns(areas)].to_numpy()
    emb = emb / np.linalg.norm(emb, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    pos = pd.Series(np.arange(len(areas)), index=areas.index)
    dist = 1 - (emb[pos[adj["focal"]]] * emb[pos[adj["neighbor"]]]).sum(axis=1)
    out = pd.Series(dist, index=pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([adj["focal"], adj["neighbor"]], names=["a", "b"]),
                    name="dist")
    if cache is not None:
        out.to_frame().to_parquet(cache)
    return out

You’re right that they look alike: from above, both sides of those pairs are dense blocks with dark roofs. The embedding does tell them apart, but I wouldn’t use them as cards.
What the model sees

Orange side (cluster 95): S01017417 and S01017427 sit well inside the business-core cluster. Their most similar areas in the whole UK are other Glasgow core zones, and S01017414’s include London and Manchester cores. To the model they’re office districts.
Green side (cluster 61): S01017432 and S01017433 belong to a tenement and terrace housing cluster. 82% of its areas fall in the k=20 “Victorian terraces” cluster. Their most similar areas are neighbouring Glasgow zones (S01017430/31) and several Northern Irish areas, which I’d guess are Belfast but haven’t checked.

So the 0.25–0.27 distance probably reflects the difference between commercial and residential use: building heights, flat versus pitched roofs, courtyard greenery. AlphaEarth mixes radar and multispectral inputs that respond to these. That’s my reading, not something I’ve tested.
Why the distance is still shaky

The areas are tiny. These zones cover 0.03–0.10 km², which is only a few hundred 10 m pixels. Roads and edges weigh heavily in their average, so their vectors are noisier than most.
The green areas are borderline members of their own cluster. S01017432 is further from its cluster centre than 98% of the other members, and S01017433 is the furthest of all. They sit on the edge of the cluster, closer to the business core than to typical tenements.
These are simply the extremes of a small pool. Pairs touching Scottish business-core areas have a median distance of 0.036. The highest is 0.268, which is pair 3. Cluster 95 has only 133 areas, so after the first two cards we’re down to subtle contrasts.

I’ve sent a contact sheet of the four Glasgow tenement zones next to their two closest Northern Irish matches. You can see they’re the same type: courtyard blocks with dark roofs.
My suggestion: keep pairs 1, 2 and 4, which show visible contrasts (fields and campus, reservoir and sheds, riverside park). Drop 3 and 5. Going forward, I’d add a cut-off for “card-worthy” pairs: a minimum distance (for example the top 0.5% of pairs, about 0.27), a minimum area so tiny zones don’t produce noise, or both.

### Dissimilarity from the whole neighbourhood

Two ways to score how different an area is from its neighbourhood as a whole, using equal weights for every neighbour:

- **`mean_dist`**: the average of the cosine distances to each neighbour, i.e. how different the area is from its neighbours one by one. Taken from the weights of `g_dist`.
- **`lag_dist`**: the cosine distance to the *average neighbour*, i.e. how different the area is from its surroundings taken together. The average neighbour is the spatial lag of the embeddings on the row-standardised graph.

Since averaging neighbours tends to cancel out their differences, `lag_dist` should be at most `mean_dist` for nearly every area. The gap between the two is roughly how much the neighbours differ among themselves.

What stands out:

Only #1 is a real outlier. After it, the cards fall to the top 3–5%, which the histogram line makes obvious.
Averaging dilutes the contrast. lag_dist compares an area with the average of its neighbours. Business cores are usually surrounded by mixed fabric, so a park on one side and dense blocks on the other cancel out. On average, lag_dist is half of mean_dist (0.026 vs 0.053).
Few neighbours and tiny areas push the score up. Most of these areas have only 2–3 neighbours, and #2 and #3 cover around 0.02 km² each. That’s the same small-area noise we saw with the Glasgow pairs.
Cards 3–5 are still good pictures even though their scores are modest. They show the “towers dropped into a neighbourhood” idea well. Card 3, with its towers by the river, is the most striking.

# #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: clustering the embeddings

The first notebook (`gdsl30dmc.ipynb`) found the UK's most dissimilar neighbouring small areas, but the top results were nearly always built-up land against open land. Here we cluster the 2024 AlphaEarth embeddings into groups of similar areas, interpret the groups visually, and then search for contrasts between *types* of place, e.g. the industrial estate next to the most different landscape. Shared data loading, contiguity and Polaroid cards come from `gdsl30dmc_tools.py`.

I’d submit two cards, with an optional third.
1. Staines reservoirs: E01030745 and E01030710, the UK’s most dissimilar neighbouring pair

Why it’s striking: two huge black reservoirs pressed against a tight grid of suburban housing. You read the contrast instantly.
What it shows: this is the headline result. At a cosine distance of 0.538 it is #1 of all 136,233 neighbouring pairs. The same area also tops mean_dist and lag_dist, so the result holds however you measure it.

2. Nene Washes: E01018058 and E01018072, ranked #32 of 136,233

Why it’s striking: it’s a puzzle. In the photo both areas look like fenland fields, yet the embeddings put them among the most different pairs in the UK, and the pair landed in the reservoirs cluster.
What it shows: I checked the location. It’s between Peterborough and Whittlesey, which matches the Nene Washes, a flood-storage washland that sits under water for much of the winter. I haven’t confirmed that against the embeddings themselves, so treat it as the likely explanation.

One photo can’t show seasonal flooding, but an embedding that summarises the whole of 2024 can. That’s exactly the case for embeddings over imagery.
On this card, the band chart (grey for what’s shared, colour for the gap) earns its place.

Correction: I called this the Ouse Washes earlier. The coordinates put it at the Nene Washes.

Optional third: Macclesfield retail park and the moors: E01018631 and E01018669

Why it’s striking: a retail and industrial park on the edge of Macclesfield, with the Peak District moorland directly beside it. It’s top 0.07% of pairs.
What it shows: it’s the cluster idea working. We asked “what’s the most different thing next to an industrial park?” and got an answer you wouldn’t find by browsing. It also avoids water, so the set isn’t three water stories.

Business-core cards: the distances are weaker, or the pictures need explaining.
Central London block next to a park: it looks lovely but is only top 0.75%.
Port cards: they have cloud in the imagery.

You’re right: to the eye they’re the same kind of place. That’s why I’d drop the Kensal pair as a submission card.
What the embeddings say:

Neither area is an outlier. Each sits comfortably inside its own k=100 cluster: E01004721 is in cluster 68 and E01004722 in cluster 69, and each is about as close to its cluster centre as a typical member. Their most similar areas elsewhere are ordinary members of the same clusters.
So this isn’t small-area noise, as it partly was in Glasgow. The model consistently separates two kinds of place, and the centres of clusters 68 and 69 are 0.299 apart. That’s as far apart as many pairs of housing and woodland.

What the imagery shows: I made sheets of 9 typical areas from each cluster, also sent. Both look like dense terraced housing. Cluster 69 is slightly more uniform Victorian terraces (94% England); cluster 68 mixes in some flats and estates, with 15% Scotland and 11% Northern Ireland. Nothing explains a gap that large.
My best guess, which I haven’t tested:

Street orientation. On the card, the orange terraces mostly run east–west and the green ones north–south.
AlphaEarth includes radar (Sentinel-1), and radar returns from buildings depend strongly on how the streets are oriented relative to the satellite’s path. This is a known effect, sometimes called the cardinal effect.
Two identical terraced grids at right angles could look very different to the model.
One way to test it: compute the dominant street direction of areas in clusters 68 and 69 from OpenStreetMap and see whether it separates them.

For the submission: a card whose main contrast we can’t explain, and which may be a sensor artefact, is risky as a showcase. I’d use Hackney Marshes as the third card instead. It sits entirely within London, ranks #103 of 136,233, and the contrast is real and easy to read.
The Kensal pair would make a good follow-up: “what are embeddings actually seeing?”

## Areas and their neighbours

We read the 2024 areas with their mean embeddings and connect every pair of areas whose polygons touch or overlap (fuzzy contiguity: queen contiguity plus the England–Scotland border, where the two nations' polygons overlap). Twelve island areas have no neighbours, so we drop them.
@@code
%%time
YEAR = 2024
areas = tools.load_areas(YEAR)
g = tools.contiguity(areas)
areas, g = tools.drop_isolates(areas, g)
print(f"{len(areas):,} areas | {g.n_edges // 2:,} neighbouring pairs")
@@markdown
## How different is each pair of neighbours?

For every neighbouring pair we compute the cosine distance between their embeddings: 0 means the two areas look the same to the model, and larger values mean more different. We compute it from scratch here (`cache=None`) rather than reading the copy cached by the exploration notebooks. Each pair appears once, with its two codes in alphabetical order.
@@code
dist = tools.pair_distances(areas, g, cache=None)
km2 = areas.area / 1e6
pairs = dist.reset_index().assign(km2_a=lambda d: km2[d.a].to_numpy(), km2_b=lambda d: km2[d.b].to_numpy())
pairs.dist.describe().round(4)
EOF

## Picking the three pairs

- **Most different:** the pair with the largest distance.
- **Most similar:** the pair with the smallest distance.
- **Most similar urban:** the smallest distance among pairs where both areas cover between 0.05 and 1 km². Areas are drawn to hold similar numbers of people, so small areas are urban. The lower bound leaves out tiny areas, whose average embedding rests on only a few hundred 10 m pixels and is less reliable.

On each card, the larger of the two areas is outlined in orange and the other in green.
@@code
URBAN_KM2 = (0.05, 1.0)
urban = pairs.km2_a.between(*URBAN_KM2) & pairs.km2_b.between(*URBAN_KM2)

picks = pd.DataFrame({
    "most_different": pairs.loc[pairs.dist.idxmax()],
    "most_similar": pairs.loc[pairs.dist.idxmin()],
    "most_similar_urban": pairs[urban].loc[pairs[urban].dist.idxmin()],
}).T
swap = picks.km2_b > picks.km2_a  # larger area first, so it is drawn in orange
picks.loc[swap, ["a", "b", "km2_a", "km2_b"]] = picks.loc[swap, ["b", "a", "km2_b", "km2_a"]].to_numpy()
picks["rank_different"] = [int((dist > d).sum()) + 1 for d in picks.dist]
picks["rank_similar"] = [int((dist < d).sum()) + 1 for d in picks.dist]
picks
EOF

Every small area in the UK, all 46,832 of them, has a 2024 [AlphaEarth](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/alphaearth-foundations-helps-map-our-planet-in-unprecedented-detail/) embedding, made available by [Imago](https://data.imago.ac.uk/datasets/google-satellite-embedding-v1-small-areas-2017-2024): 64 numbers that sum up a year of satellite observations of the place. Compare each area with the ones it touches and you get 136,233 pairs of neighbours, which we can rank from most different to most alike.

These are three of them.

::: {.prints}
[![](images/submission/1_most_different.jpg){.print fig-alt="Staines Reservoirs next to the streets of Stanwell, Surrey: the most different neighbouring pair in the UK."}](images/submission/1_most_different.jpg)

[![](images/submission/2_most_similar.jpg){.print fig-alt="Two stretches of farmland in County Armagh: the most similar neighbouring pair in the UK."}](images/submission/2_most_similar.jpg)

[![](images/submission/3_most_similar_urban.jpg){.print fig-alt="Two halves of the same terraced streets in Ilford, east London: the most similar urban neighbours."}](images/submission/3_most_similar_urban.jpg)
:::

**The most different:** Staines Reservoirs and the streets of Stanwell next door, #1 of 136,233 pairs.<br>
**The most alike:** two stretches of farmland in County Armagh.<br>
**The most alike in a city:** two halves of the same terraced streets in Ilford.

The first is the one you'd guess. The other two are more interesting: the boundaries we use to count people often split places that, as far as the satellites can tell, are the same place.

## Reading a card

Each card is a Polaroid of one pair of neighbouring areas. The two areas are outlined in orange and green over Esri satellite imagery, and everything else is washed out. Underneath are the areas' official codes, the place, the cosine distance between their embeddings (0 means identical; the largest in the UK is 0.538) and its rank among all pairs. The UK locator shows where the pair is. The haiku says what the numbers can't.

The submission is three cards, but it took {{< var n_prompts >}} prompts over {{< var n_days >}} days to get there. This is the route, chapter by chapter. Each chapter quotes the prompts that turned the corner: the typed notes are the human's words, unedited, and their numbers link to the exact spot in the [transcript](transcript.qmd). The images are what Claude looked at along the way, most of which never made it into a notebook.

## 1 · The brief

The project started from a short brief, `SPEC.md`: map the UK's most dissimilar neighbouring small areas, measuring similarity with AlphaEarth embeddings from [Imago](https://data.imago.ac.uk/datasets/google-satellite-embedding-v1-small-areas-2017-2024), using geopandas and PySAL's new `Graph`, and keeping a log of explorations.

{{< include _generated/prompt-1.md >}}

## 2 · Who touches whom

Before comparing neighbours, we need to know who the neighbours are. Queen contiguity (areas sharing at least a corner) across all four nations gave a graph with one surprise: no links at all across the England–Scotland border, because the two nations' polygons overlap rather than touch. Fuzzy contiguity, which also counts overlaps, fixed that with 21 extra links. Twelve island areas had no neighbours at all and were dropped.

{{< include _generated/prompt-2.md >}}
{{< include _generated/prompt-6.md >}}

::: {.polaroid .tilt-l}
![](conversation/img/001.jpg)
[The twelve areas with no neighbours, all of them Scottish islands.]{.caption}
:::

## 3 · Measuring difference

Each area's embedding is a 64-number vector; the difference between two neighbours is the cosine distance between their vectors, computed for all 136,233 neighbouring pairs. The human pushed for splitting the work into 16 chunks, one per core, which (after a detour about threads versus processes and memory layout) made it fast.

{{< include _generated/prompt-11.md >}}
{{< include _generated/prompt-13.md >}}

We also scored each area against its whole neighbourhood, in two ways: the average distance to each neighbour (`mean_dist`), and the distance to the average neighbour (`lag_dist`).

{{< include _generated/prompt-18.md >}}

## 4 · Finding a look

The first maps were plain: satellite imagery with the area and its neighbours outlined. Then came a long stretch of iteration on the look, which became the Polaroid card used on every map since.

**The most different:** Staines Reservoirs and the streets of Stanwell next door, #1 of 136,233 pairs.<br>
**The most alike:** two stretches of farmland in County Armagh.<br>
**The most alike in a city:** two halves of the same terraced streets in Ilford.

The first is the one you'd guess. The other two are more interesting: the boundaries we use to count people often split places that, as far as the satellites can tell, are the same place.

## Reading a card

Each card is a Polaroid of one pair of neighbouring areas. The two areas are outlined in orange and green over Esri satellite imagery, and everything else is washed out. Underneath are the areas' official codes, the place, the cosine distance between their embeddings (0 means identical; the largest in the UK is 0.538) and its rank among all pairs. The UK locator shows where the pair is. The haiku says what the numbers can't.

All the analysis lives in three Jupyter notebooks and one shared Python module. Claude wrote and ran them, cell by cell, through the [`nb`](https://github.com/jupyter-ai-contrib/nb-cli) command-line tool ({{< var n_nb >}} `nb` commands in the [transcript](transcript.qmd)). They are shown here with the outputs saved when they were last run; the site doesn't re-run them.

[1 · Neighbours and distances](gdsl30dmc.ipynb) (`gdsl30dmc.ipynb`)
: Reads the 2024 areas and embeddings, builds the neighbour graph (fuzzy contiguity, fixing the England–Scotland border), drops the 12 islands, computes the cosine distance for every neighbouring pair in parallel, scores each area against its neighbourhood (`mean_dist`, `lag_dist`), and makes the first Polaroid cards of the most different areas and pairs.

[2 · Clusters and entities](gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb) (`gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb`)
: Clusters the embeddings with k-means at k=20 and k=100, labels them with contact sheets, then searches for contrasts by type: business cores, reservoirs, industrial estates, golf courses, woodland, harbours. Also where the histogram and embedding band charts were developed, and where the west London housing puzzle is written up.

[3 · The submission, end to end](gdsl30dmc_submission.ipynb) (`gdsl30dmc_submission.ipynb`)
: The short, standalone pipeline behind the three cards: data → neighbours → distances → three pairs picked by rule → captions and haiku → cards. Start here if you want to reproduce the submission.

`gdsl30dmc_tools.py`
: The shared module: data loading, contiguity, distance caches, and the Polaroid card template (`polaroid`, `pair_card`, `area_card`) with its options (histogram, embedding band chart, haiku).

title: Log
text: Claude kept this log in LOG.md throughout the project, adding an entry only when the human asked for one. It’s the most compact record of what was tried, the numbers behind each decision and the dead ends. It’s included here as it stands in the repository (without its own title).

title: Log
text:
2026-11-04 — Contiguity graph (all four nations, queen)
Data (2024): 46,844 small areas — England 33,755 LSOAs, Scotland 7,392 Data Zones, Northern Ireland 3,780 Super Data Zones, Wales 1,917 LSOAs. EPSG:27700, 64 embedding bands (band{1..64}_mean), no missing values. Embedding vector lengths are 0.75–0.99 rather than 1, because they are averages of unit-length pixel vectors.
Queen contiguity (Graph.build_contiguity(lsoas, rook=False), ~18 s): 272,424 links (counted in both directions), but only 1 England–Scotland pair. Wales–England looked fine (99 links each way). strict=True was worse: zero England–Scotland links, and 326 fewer within Northern Ireland.
Diagnosis: polygons within 1 m of each other show ~23 England–Scotland pairs, all at distance 0, which overlap by up to ~70,000 m² (the two nations’ boundaries come from different sources). Contiguity requires polygons to touch without overlapping, so these links are dropped.
Fix: Graph.build_fuzzy_contiguity(lsoas), which links any polygons that intersect (~3 s). It contains every queen link plus the 21 missing England–Scotland pairs (23 in total), and nothing else changed.
Final graph g: 272,466 links, median 6 neighbours per area (max 53), 12 areas with no neighbours, 31 disconnected pieces (mainland GB 42,777; Northern Ireland 3,779; island groups, largest 89). The areas with no neighbours need handling before we compute dissimilarity.

title: Log
text:
2026-11-04 — Dropped areas with no neighbours
Removed the 12 areas with no neighbours from both g (g.subgraph) and lsoas/emb: E01019077, S01014306, S01014332, S01014346, S01019112, S01019115, S01019116, S01019117, S01019737, S01019747, S01019748, N20001651. Island groups with several areas were kept. Result: 46,832 areas, 272,466 links (unchanged), 19 disconnected pieces (was 31).

title: Log
text:
2026-11-04 — Isolates figure
Added a figure of the 12 dropped areas (overview + one zoomed panel each) to the notebook, plotting only those areas on contextily tiles to keep it light. CartoDB tiles now require an API key (they return “API key required” placeholders), so we use cx.providers.Esri.WorldGrayCanvas (no key needed). All 12 are offshore islands (Scilly, Inner Hebrides, Orkney, Shetland, Rathlin). Note: nb execute gives each cell 30 s by default; the full notebook needs --timeout 300.

title: Log
text:
2026-11-04 — Neighbour dissimilarity (cosine)
Measure: cosine distance between the 64-band embeddings of every pair of neighbours in g (fuzzy contiguity), via sklearn.metrics.pairwise.paired_cosine_distances. Chosen over Euclidean because the area vectors are averages of unit-length vectors: their length partly reflects how mixed the land cover is, and cosine ignores it. Each pair is computed in both directions (272,466 values). Results are stored as weights of g_dist = graph.Graph(Series(dist, index=g.adjacency.index)).
Parallelism: the areas are split into 16 groups by focal area (one per core), and each group’s pair distances are computed on a separate thread (joblib backend="threading"), then written back in the original order. Benchmark (scratch): serial ~1 s; separate processes (loky) were slower (1.6–2.2 s, because each worker has to be sent its share of the data); threads were ~4–8× faster. Bigger win: lsoas[band_cols].to_numpy() stores values column by column, so picking out whole rows is slow; np.ascontiguousarray(emb) cut the threaded step from ~0.66 s to ~0.16 s. The full notebook cell still takes ~0.75 s (not investigated). Checked: every pair computed once, matches the serial result, same structure as g.
Distribution: median 0.032, IQR 0.016–0.068, mean 0.054, max 0.54. Strongly right-skewed: most neighbours are similar, with a long tail of very different pairs.

title: Log
text:
2026-11-04 — Neighbourhood dissimilarity: mean_dist vs lag_dist
Two per-area scores, with equal weights for every neighbour: mean_dist = mean of the cosine distances to each neighbour (g_dist.aggregate("mean")); lag_dist = cosine distance to the average neighbour embedding (g.transform("r").lag(emb)). lag_dist <= mean_dist for every area. Spearman rank correlation 0.84. Medians 0.046 vs 0.017, max 0.456 vs 0.438. In the scatter plot, areas near the diagonal are outliers (unlike all their surroundings); areas well below it are transitions (their neighbours differ from each other). Also built most_dissimilar: each area’s single most dissimilar neighbour and the distance to it.
Top area on both measures: E01030745, a pair of reservoir basins just south of Heathrow, surrounded by housing/industry/airport (distances to those neighbours 0.39–0.54); its only similar neighbour (0.16) is the large reservoir to the west. Expect other water/coast cases near the top of the ranking.

title: Log
text:
2026-11-04 — Map template (style “C1”)
Iterated in the scratchpad: map of a focal area + its neighbours over satellite imagery, comparing 4 fades (dark, washed, greyscale, navy) × 5 line palettes, then an Imago-palette grid (colours taken from imago.ac.uk CSS: indigo #24226f/#181651, orange #ff8f42, teal #03cea3, lilac #a9afff, grey-lavender #8c91a8, amber #ffaf39). Chosen: C1 = Esri.WorldImagery; outside the focal area + neighbours washed to white (55%); focal outline orange, neighbours teal, both with a faint dark outline; UK locator inset with no box in Imago indigo with an orange dot.
Implementation (notebook, plot_focal(code)): fetch tiles once with cx.bounds2img and reproject to EPSG:27700 with cx.warp_tiles. The wash is applied to the image pixels with a mask from shapely.contains_xy against the merged outline of the focal area and its neighbours (this also allows effects like greyscale, which an overlay polygon can’t do). Attribution uses the provider’s own string.
UK outline for the inset: merging all 46k polygons took ~8 min. shapely.coverage_union_all on everything fails (the polygons overlap at national borders), so: merge each nation with coverage union (England 0.4 s, Scotland 3 s, Wales <0.1 s; Northern Ireland isn’t cleanly tiled → falls back to union_all on 200 m-simplified polygons), then join the four nations, drop holes and parts under 20 km², and simplify by 1.5 km. ~26 s total.

The strip has the area code (22 pt) and mean_dist · lag_dist · n neighbours (11 pt) in bold Figtree (static TTFs from github.com/erikdkennedy/figtree, OFL, saved in fonts/, registered with font_manager.addfont), the Esri credit in regular weight, and the UK silhouette at bottom right. title: Log
text:
2026-11-04 — Top 5 areas per measure
mean_dist and lag_dist give the same top 5 in the same order: E01030745 (0.456/0.438, 9 neighbours), N20003012 (0.381/0.374, 4), W01001286 (0.375/0.360, 3), N20002748 (0.355/0.353, 3), E01026177 (0.315/0.308, 2). Cards exported to figures/<code>.png. Ranks 2–5 are the reverse of the reservoir case: small built-up cores (town/village) inside a few large rural neighbours (farmland, moorland/forestry, coastal peninsula, woodland). True but not very interesting. Observations: (1) the top areas have few neighbours (2–4 vs median 6), so their averages rest on a handful of pairs; (2) with large rural neighbours the focal area is tiny on the card. Decision: switch from whole neighbourhoods to individual pairs of neighbours.

title: Log
text:
2026-11-04 — Pairs section + pair Polaroid cards
New section “Most dissimilar neighbouring pairs”: one row per pair (area_a < area_b), 136,233 pairs. In the raw top 20, the reservoir E01030745 appears 7 times (only 32 distinct areas). Distinct pairs: go down the ranking and skip any pair that shares an area with a pair already chosen. Top 5: E01030710–E01030745 (0.538), E01031353–E01031359 (0.513), E01020936–E01034298 (0.503), E01029178–E01035125 (0.484), W01001947–W01002024 (0.481).
Template refactor: generic polaroid(layers, title, subtitle, locate) (layers = list of (gdf, colour, lw), which set the frame and stay unwashed; a title item with a colour gets a short bar in that colour before it). plot_focal(code) (unchanged look) and new plot_pair(a, b) (A orange, B green, both 2.4 pt; caption “A ▬ B ▬” + cosine distance) are thin wrappers. Exports: figures/pair_<a>_<b>.png.
Observations: most top pairs are again a strong contrast between built-up and open land (housing vs reservoir, village vs farmland, coastal town vs farmed headland, industrial/retail vs open water). In one card (E01020936–E01034298) Esri’s imagery has clouds; Esri’s imagery is a recent mosaic, not the 2024 imagery the embeddings were built from. In some pairs one area is tiny relative to the other (e.g. E01035125).

section: 2026-11-04 — Ideas for more interesting cards + choosing k
text:
2026-11-04 — Ideas for more interesting cards + choosing k
Pair cards were one-note (built-up vs open land every time). Two ideas: (1) restrict the search to cities (needs boundaries: ONS area→local-authority lookup recommended, or built-up-area polygons); (2) cluster the embeddings, interpret the clusters visually, then search at cluster level (top pair per cluster combination, and “surprising neighbours”, i.e. cluster pairs adjacent less often than chance). Plan: do (2) first, then (1) as a filter on top.

Silhouette falls steadily with no peak or elbow: the embeddings form continuous gradients, so k is a choice about interpretability, not a statistical answer. Decision: k=20 for labelling (190 cluster pairs, all clusters ≥835 areas), and also record each area’s k=50 cluster to keep the rare types. So the sharp drop in smallest-cluster size sits between k=50 and k=75 there (the scratch run put it at 40→50, with 89 at k=50): its position is sensitive to the isolates and the random start. The fine level (k=50 vs k=75) is still open. Development moves to a second notebook, gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb; shared tooling moved to gdsl30dmc_tools.py.

section: 2026-11-05 — Clusters (k=20, k=100), business cores and new card options
text:
2026-11-05 — Clusters (k=20, k=100), business cores and new card options
Clustering (gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb): the user chose k=20 and k=100 (this settles the “fine level still open” note above). k-means on vectors scaled to length 1, n_init=10, clusters numbered by size (0 = largest); labels saved to data/clusters_2024.parquet. k=20 sizes 837–3,628; k=100 sizes 71–869. The two levels nest only loosely (median share of a k=100 cluster inside its main k=20 cluster: 0.61). Contact sheets of the 6 most typical areas (closest to the centre) per k=20 cluster: figures/clusters/c20_XX.png. Draft labels: about 12 of 20 clusters are shades of residential; non-residential types are city centres/dense mixed use (18), arable (8), mixed farmland (10), pastoral (11), woodland/parkland fringe (17), uplands (19). No industrial or water cluster at k=20. Clusters 1, 5 and 12 are mostly Scottish/NI urban areas (England has 72% of all areas): real building styles, an embedding effect, or Data Zone size; flagged as a caveat.
Business cores. k=20 cluster 18 is broader than “city centres” (dense inner-city mixed use: flats, offices, institutions). At k=100, City of London and central Manchester areas fall into cluster 95 (6 of 10 checked) and 88 (4 of 10). Cluster 95 is the high-rise office district (133 areas, median 0.11 km², E 114 / S 17 / N 2, 65% inside k=20 cluster 18); 88 is central mixed use. Focus on 95. - Pairs (563 neighbouring pairs include a core area; top 5 distinct, core area in orange): E01035620–E01035617 (0.408, fields + campus, top 0.03% of all 136,233 pairs), E01034486–E01004401 (0.289, reservoir + sheds), S01017417–S01017432 (0.268), S01017414–S01017176 (0.257, riverside park), S01017427–S01017433 (0.254). The two weak Glasgow pairs (3, 5) look alike from above: the core areas match other business cores and the neighbours a tenement cluster (c100 61), so the gap is plausibly offices vs flats; but the neighbours are tiny (0.06–0.10 km²) and at the edge of their cluster. Suggested filter for card-worthy pairs: minimum distance and/or minimum area. - lag_dist (top 5 core areas): only E01034486 (0.180, the reservoir block, top 0.29% of areas) is a clear outlier; the rest are top 3–5% (averaging neighbours dilutes contrast; most have 2–3 neighbours, some ~0.02 km²). Cards 3–5 still show towers set into neighbourhoods well. - Cards: figures/core/pair_<i>_<a>_<b>.png, figures/core/lag_<i>_<code>.png; contact sheet figures/clusters/c100_95.png.
Card options (gdsl30dmc_tools.py): - pair_distances() and neighbourhood_distances() compute every neighbouring-pair distance and per-area mean_dist/lag_dist once, cached to data/pair_distances_2024.parquet and data/neighbourhood_distances_2024.parquet (match notebook 1). - hist=True (pairs) or hist="lag_dist"/"mean_dist": slim histogram of the measure over the whole dataset in the caption strip, the card’s value marked with a line and “top x% of N”. The distribution is very skewed (median pair 0.032, max 0.538). - emb=(orange_vector, green_vector): band-by-band chart of the two embeddings, one column per band (1–64). Styles tried: "paired" (side by side; reads as texture), "overlay" (transparent; overlap turns a muddy teal), "diff" (orange minus green; clean but loses the values), "shared" (default): the part both share in light Imago grey and only the excess coloured, so more grey = more alike. For lag cards, green is the average neighbour. The band chart replaces the histogram; with both, the caption strip grows to fit (card 10.1 in tall instead of 9.55).

Entity scan (clusters notebook, “Distinct entities at k=100”): contact sheets of all 100 fine clusters (4 typical areas each, 9 for candidates). Most are shades of housing, farmland or fringe. Clearly delimited entities: 99 reservoirs/inland water (71 areas), 81 industrial and transport land, 50 industrial and retail parks, 42 golf courses and leafy suburbs, 91 woodland and heathland, 90 harbour/marina waterfront, 87 port and coastal industrial towns, 93 coastal fringe, 95 business cores, 88 central mixed use. Landscapes: 97 Highland mountains, 98 Scottish islands, 94 Scottish uplands, 85 English/Welsh uplands, 92 Welsh valleys. Not found: airports, quarries, campuses, cemeteries, stand-alone docks (probably smaller than a typical area). Labels are a visual reading, not ground truth.
Top 3 pairs per entity (both areas ≥ 0.05 km², distinct, entity area first; 27 cards in figures/entities/, shared band chart). Highlights: 99 #1 Staines (#1 of all pairs), 99 #3 Nene Washes (fields in the photo, water cluster in the embedding: likely seasonal flooding of the washland; #22), 50 #2 Macclesfield retail park vs Peak District moors (#102), 88 central London blocks vs royal parks. gdsl30dmc_submission.ipynb, a new standalone notebook that runs start to end (~2 min): load areas → fuzzy contiguity → drop 12 isolates → pair distances computed from scratch (cache=None) → pick the three pairs by rule → captions (guarded by expect codes, so a changed pick stops the run) → cards at 200 dpi in figures/submission/ (1_most_different, 2_most_similar, 3_most_similar_urban). Post text: the LinkedIn text for the three cards (brief, plain, no buzzwords) is the last section of gdsl30dmc_submission.ipynb (“Post text”), kept in a plain-text block so the hashtags don’t render as headings. It covers: the AlphaEarth embeddings via Imago, 46,832 areas and 136,233 neighbouring pairs, the three pairs, and the point that the boundaries we use to count people often split places the satellites see as one. It also says everything was made by prompting Claude Code (day 10 theme: prompting only).

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: clustering the embeddings
text: The first notebook (gdsl30dmc.ipynb) found the UK’s most dissimilar neighbouring small areas, but the top results were nearly always built-up land against open land. Here we cluster the 2024 AlphaEarth embeddings into groups of similar areas, interpret the groups visually, and then search for contrasts between types of place, e.g. the industrial estate next to the most different landscape. Shared data loading, contiguity and Polaroid cards come from gdsl30dmc_tools.py.

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: clustering the embeddings
text:
Setup
Libraries for this notebook: scikit-learn for k-means and silhouette scores, plus the shared gdsl30dmc_tools module. autoreload picks up edits to the module without restarting the kernel.


code
%load_ext autoreload
%autoreload 2

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

import gdsl30dmc_tools as tools

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: clustering the embeddings
text:
Reading data
We load the 2024 areas and build the same neighbour graph as in the first notebook: fuzzy contiguity, which is queen contiguity plus the overlapping England–Scotland border pairs. We drop the 12 island areas with no neighbours. Each embedding vector is scaled to length 1, so that k-means, which works with Euclidean distance, effectively groups areas by cosine similarity, the same measure used in the first notebook.


code
%%time
YEAR = 2024
lsoas = tools.load_areas(YEAR)
g = tools.contiguity(lsoas)
lsoas, g = tools.drop_isolates(lsoas, g)

emb = np.ascontiguousarray(lsoas[tools.band_columns(lsoas)].to_numpy())
emb_unit = emb / np.linalg.norm(emb, axis=1, keepdims=True)
uk_outline = tools.uk_outline(lsoas)

Choosing the number of clusters
Before fixing k, we fit k-means for a range of values and record two things: the silhouette score (how well separated the clusters are, from −1 to 1, computed with cosine distance on a 10,000-area sample) and the size of the smallest cluster. There’s no single right k here: the aim is a number of groups we can label by eye that still keeps rare land types visible.

We use k=20 to label the main groups (190 possible pairs of cluster types, every cluster with at least ~840 areas) and also record a finer level to keep the rare types visible.

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: clustering the embeddings
text:
Clustering the embeddings
We fit k-means at two levels: k=20 for the main land types we’ll label by eye, and k=100 for a finer split that should separate rarer types. We use 10 random starts per fit for stability, and number the clusters in each level by size (0 = largest), so the numbering stays meaningful. The labels are saved to data/clusters_2024.parquet for reuse.


code
%%time
def fit_kmeans(k, seed=0):
    km = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=seed).fit(emb_unit)
    order = np.argsort(-np.bincount(km.labels_))  # old label of the largest cluster first
    relabel = np.empty(k, int)
    relabel[order] = np.arange(k)
    return relabel[km.labels_], km.cluster_centers_[order]

c20, centres20 = fit_kmeans(20)
c100, centres100 = fit_kmeans(100)
clusters = pd.DataFrame({"c20": c20, "c100": c100}, index=lsoas.index)
clusters.to_parquet(tools.DATA_DIR / f"clusters_{YEAR}.parquet")

print("k=100 sizes: min", np.bincount(c100).min(), "| median", int(np.median(np.bincount(c100))), "| max", np.bincount(c100).max())

title: #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: clustering the embeddings
text:
What the clusters look like
To interpret each k=20 cluster, we look at its six most typical areas: those whose embedding is closest (highest cosine similarity) to the cluster centre. Each is shown as a satellite thumbnail with the area outlined and its surroundings washed out. The sheets are saved to figures/clusters/ so we can review them side by side and agree labels.


code
def typical(level_labels, centres, cluster, n=6):
    """Codes of the n areas in `cluster` closest to its centre (cosine similarity)."""
    members = np.flatnonzero(level_labels == cluster)
    centre = centres[cluster] / np.linalg.norm(centres[cluster])
    best = members[np.argsort(-(emb_unit[members] @ centre))[:n]]
    return lsoas.index[best].tolist()

typical20 = {c: typical(c20, centres20, c) for c in range(20)}

text:
Business cores (k=100 cluster 95)
The k=20 cluster we first read as “city centres” (cluster 18) turned out broader: dense inner-city mixed use, with flats, offices and institutions. To find true city centres we look at the k=100 level instead. Areas in the City of London and central Manchester fall into k=100 clusters 95 and 88. The contact sheets show that cluster 95 is the high-rise office district: towers, big flat roofs and almost no green space. Cluster 88 is central mixed use, so we focus on 95 and call it the business core cluster.

Business cores next to their most different neighbours
We take the cosine distance of every neighbouring pair (computed once and cached by tools.pair_distances) and keep the pairs that include a business-core area, with the core area listed first. As in the first notebook, we pick the top pairs greedily, skipping any pair that shares an area with one already chosen. The neighbour’s k=20 and k=100 clusters show what kind of place the core sits against.


code
pair_dist = tools.pair_distances(lsoas, g)
assert len(pair_dist) == g.n_edges // 2

core_pairs = pair_dist.reset_index()
in_a, in_b = core_pairs.a.isin(core), core_pairs.b.isin(core)
core_pairs = core_pairs[in_a | in_b]
swap = ~in_a[core_pairs.index]  # put the core area first
core_pairs.loc[swap, ["a", "b"]] = core_pairs.loc[swap, ["b", "a"]].to_numpy()
core_pairs = core_pairs.sort_values("dist", ascending=False)

used, picks = set(), []
for row in core_pairs.itertuples():
    if row.a in used or row.b in used:

    rank=lambda d: [f"top {(pair_dist >= x).mean():.2%}" for x in d.dist])

Most dissimilar neighbours of each entity
For each entity (except business cores, covered above), the top 3 distinct neighbouring pairs that include one of its areas, with the entity area first. To avoid the small-area noise seen in Glasgow, both areas must cover at least 0.05 km². The rank is among all 136,233 neighbouring pairs. Cards are saved to figures/entities/.


code
MIN_KM2 = 0.05
km2 = lsoas.area / 1e6
pair_rank = lambda d: int((pair_dist > d).sum()) + 1

def top_pairs(members, n=3, min_km2=MIN_KM2):
    """Top n distinct neighbouring pairs that include an area in `members`, member first, both areas >= min_km2."""
    p = pair_dist.reset_index()
    in_a, in_b = p.a.isin(members), p.b.isin(members)
    p = p[in_a | in_b]
    swap = ~in_a[p.index]
    p.loc[swap, ["a", "b"]] = p.loc[swap, ["b", "a"]].to_numpy()
    p = p[(km2[p.a].to_numpy() >= min_km2) & (km2[p.b].to_numpy() >= min_km2)].sort_values("dist", ascending=False)
    used, picks = set(), []
    for row in p.itertuples():
        if row.a in used or row.b in used:
            continue
        picks.append(row)
        used |= {row.a, row.b}
        if len(picks) == n:
            break
    return pd.DataFrame(picks).drop(columns="Index")

entity_pairs = pd.concat({
    k: top_pairs(set(clusters.index[clusters.c100 == k])) for k in ENTITIES if k != 95
}, names=["c100", "i"]).reset_index()
entity_pairs["i"] += 1
entity_pairs["rank"] = entity_pairs.dist.map(pair_rank)
entity_pairs["nbr_c100"] = clusters.c100[entity_pairs.b].to_numpy()

Highlights:

Reservoirs #1 is the Staines reservoirs pair, the most dissimilar in the UK.
Reservoirs #3 looks like ordinary fenland fields but sits in the water cluster. It is on the Nene Washes, a flood-storage washland that is likely under water for much of the winter, which a single photo cannot show but a year-long embedding can.
Industrial and retail parks #2 is a retail park on the edge of Macclesfield set against Peak District moorland.
Central mixed use pairs (central London blocks next to the royal parks) look striking even though their distances are lower.

Caveats:

The same pair can appear under two entities (open water next to a business park in Cardiff Bay appears under both 99 and 50).
Clouds show in a few Esri images.



A warning: similar-looking housing
Restricting the search to pairs where both areas are under 2 km² keeps it inside towns. Most top pairs there are still housing against urban open space (marshes, commons, forest). One exception, E01004721–E01004722 in west London (distance 0.317, #419), is two areas of dense terraced housing that look alike from above.
Neither is an outlier: each is a typical member of its own k=100 cluster (68 and 69), and those two clusters’ centres are 0.299 apart, as far as many housing–woodland pairs. Contact sheets of both clusters show dense terraces either way.
An untested hypothesis is street orientation. The two grids run roughly at right angles, and AlphaEarth includes radar (Sentinel-1), whose returns from buildings depend strongly on their orientation relative to the satellite track. Since we can’t explain the gap, this pair is not used as a showcase card; it is a candidate follow-up (“what do embeddings actually see?”).
